title: Introduction to Loss Functions
learning_outcomes: Explain introduction to loss functions and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study introduction to loss functions in the context of machine learning fundamentals. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Introduction to Loss Functions matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Training is only one step: a robust workflow defines splits, baselines, metrics, assumptions, and monitoring.

items.title: Prediction errors

items.text: Check the edge cases for regression loss: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by introduction to loss functions. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.code:
actual = [3, 5, 8]
predicted = [4, 4, 7]
mae = sum(abs(a-p) for a,p in zip(actual,predicted))/len(actual)
print("MAE:", round(mae, 2))

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Always compare with a simple baseline and choose a metric that fits the use case.
